newsitem.title: Australia: Australian bond yields drift higher in slow market.
newsitem.headline: Australian bond yields drift higher in slow market.

text.p: *Australian bond yields drifted higher during a relatively thin morning session with activity seen picking up later in the week once a rush of data emerges locally and in the U.S.
*RBA's Grenville confident inflation will stay low.

Australian bond yields drifted higher during a relatively thin morning session, and activity is not expected to pick up markedly until later in the week once a rush of data emerges both locally and from the U.S.
"It's all going to happen in the second half of the week, and for now it's probably going to be a question of tracking the U.S.," said one trader.
The morning's weaker tone was largely due to softness seen in U.S. Treasuries at the tail end of last week when Australian markets were closed for the ANZAC Day holiday weekend.

Treasury Corp of Victoria (TCV) issued A$100 million in its September 2001 by tender this morning. Traders said the offering was well-received, fetching a weighted average yield of 7.2843 percent after successful bids came in a one basis point range.
There was also some talk that the Australian Treasury would hold a bond tender this week, but this proved incorrect as no announcement made at midday.

Meanwhile, Reserve Bank deputy governor Stephen Grenville told a conference that he was confident that Australian inflation would remain low, but only through continuing viligance of the monetary authorities.

Data release last week showed headline CPI annual inflation at a four-year low in the March quarter at 1.3 percent and the underlying rate at 2.1 percent and within the Reserve Bank's 2.0-3.0 percent target range.

The data, combined with the moderate outcome to the "living wage" case, prompted some speculation about a further easing by the RBA, although there will be an indication of current activity with March building approvals and retail trade last this week, as well as the first quarter average weekly earnings.
The U.S. also releases a barrage of key data this week, ending with April non-farm payrolls on Friday.

Spreads widened from an initial narrowing bias against the dollar bloc. The short end of the New Zealand curve remains buoyed by a rising N.Z. TWI. Canadian debt was undermined by a weakening Canadian dollar on Friday, prior to Canadian PM Jean Chretien calling a June 2 general election on Sunday.
